forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

news_drafts.headline: Eight risks in Essex Council pension fund remain above target levels
news_drafts.lead: Essex Council's pension fund invests money on behalf of the council's employees and former employees. According to the council's quarterly investment update for the period ending 31 August 2026, all eight risks identified in the fund's risk register — potential threats to how effectively the fund can achieve its investment objectives — remain above their target levels. No new risks emerged during the quarter. The council's treasury team continues reviewing mitigation actions to address them, but the fact that all eight risks remain elevated indicates ongoing concerns about how the fund's investments are properly governed and managed.
news_drafts.paper_title: Update on Pension Fund Activity: Quarterly Investment Update Report

news_drafts.headline: Essex records 11,602 outstanding defects on principal roads, more than ten times the target
news_drafts.lead: Essex recorded 11,602 outstanding defects (unfixed repairs) on its principal roads — the network classified as most important — against a target of fewer than 1,000, according to the council's Highways Performance report for the year ending March 2026. The backlog has grown 51 per cent over the past year, from 7,689 defects in April 2025, and the council missed its target in every month tracked. Local roads face similar pressure: 16,994 outstanding defects against a target of fewer than 5,000, up from 15,600 a year earlier. The sustained rise on both networks suggests the council's maintenance capacity is under strain.

news_drafts.headline: Essex funds new carers strategy with reserve draw, but flags risk to ongoing grants
news_drafts.lead: Essex council has approved a new all-ages carers strategy funded partly by drawing down £1.6m from its Adults Investment Reserve in the coming year. However, the strategy relies on the Better Care Fund—a government grant that finances £4.26m of its £5.82m three-year cost—continuing beyond this year. The council's own papers explicitly flag that the fund "will reduce, or conditions change in future years as part of reforms". From the second year onwards, the Better Care Fund covers 77 per cent of the annual cost. The council says any reduction in that funding "will need to be managed by partners within the overall pooled budget", but sets out no fallback plan. The financial model also assumes a £68k annual saving from reduced demand for formal care assessments, though the council notes this "will need to be monitored"—despite Carers Direct Payments having grown to £2.7m in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Both police and fire paid staff significantly more than forecast, with police paying 3.5% against 2.5% assumed (£2.0m cost) and fire paying 3.8% against 2.2% (£0.7m cost)
findings.detail: Police received 3.5% officer pay award with equivalent assumed for staff, creating £2.0m additional cost versus the prior 2.5% assumption. Fire received 3.8% award for operational staff with equivalent assumed for non-operational, creating £0.7m cost against 2.2% forecast. Together this is £2.7m in unfunded pay pressures across the two services.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 70-80% of police and fire budgets. If settlements are consistently 1-1.6pp above forecast, this pattern will persist and erode future-year resilience. The MTFS assumes 2.5% police pay in 2027/28 and 2% thereafter; if actual awards exceed this, the published medium-term position is already unaffordable.
findings.figures: Police: 3.5% award, £2.0m additional cost; Fire: 3.8% award, £0.7m additional cost; combined £2.7m
findings.quote: An increase of (£2.0m) due to a 3.5% officer pay award and an assumed equivalent for staff. An increase of (£0.7m) based on a 3.8% pay award agreed for operational staff which has also been assumed for non-operational staff.

findings.headline: Fire moved from balanced 2027/28 budget in February to £0.5m shortfall by September, with £0.7m cost from a 3.8% pay award exceeding the 2.2% assumption
findings.detail: February 2026 MTFS showed balanced budget for 2027/28. September 2026 revision showed £0.5m shortfall after pay award of 3.8% (versus 2.2% assumed), costing £0.7m, plus £0.3m unbudgeted on-call costs. The shortfall persists through the medium-term outlook at £0.3m for 2029/30.
findings.matters: Fire deteriorated in opposite direction to police and faces persistent multi-year shortfalls. This is the inverse of police's one-year accounting benefit and reflects a real operational cost pressure that will need addressing through savings or reserves.
findings.figures: From balanced to £0.5m shortfall; £0.7m cost from 3.8% pay award
findings.quote: For the 2027/28 baseline budget it showed the balanced position had moved from a balanced position to a shortfall of (£0.5m) due to updated assumptions which included: An increase of (£0.7m) based on a 3.8% pay award agreed for operational staff which has also been assumed for non-operational staff.

findings.headline: Police identified £3.4m in new service demands that cannot be contained within existing budgets
findings.detail: Section 4.3 lists an increase of £3.4m for new demand and budget growth to meet increased service requirements. This was factored into the September 2026 baseline but appears as ongoing pressure in the medium-term outlook, with shortfalls appearing from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: Unaddressed demand growth of this scale signals a capacity problem that will require either budget growth, service cuts, or reserve depletion in future years. A lender would see this as a structural pressure point.
findings.quote: An increase of (£3.4m) in new demand and budget growth to meet increased service requirements which cannot be contained within existing budgets.

findings.headline: Police turned £1.4m shortfall into £0.7m surplus in four months, but £2.8m of the £2.1m swing comes from an accounting change to Minimum Revenue Provision methodology
findings.detail: June 2026 MTFS projected £1.4m shortfall in 2027/28. September 2026 revision showed £0.7m surplus after £2.1m improvement. Of this, £2.8m was "a reduction of £2.8m in the revenue costs of borrowing for the capital programme following a change in methodology in calculating the Minimum Revenue Provision to better reflect the pattern of economic benefit over the asset life." The remaining £2.1m improvement comes from pay modelling revisions (£1.8m saving, partially offset by new demand), savings identified (£1.6m), and one-off items (£0.4m), but these are offset by £3.4m new demand pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to distinguish between accounting adjustments and underlying operational improvement. A £2.8m swing from a single methodology change means the apparent improvement masks deterioration in service delivery headroom, which then appears again in the medium-term outlook where police enters deficit from 2028/29.
findings.figures: £1.4m shortfall (June) to £0.7m surplus (September) = £2.1m improvement; £2.8m of this is MRP methodology change
findings.quote: For the 2027/28 baseline budget, it showed a surplus of £0.7m compared to the previous £1.4m shortfall. The improvement of £2.1m was due to updated assumptions... A reduction of £2.8m in the revenue costs of borrowing for the capital programme following a change in methodology in calculating the Minimum Revenue Provision to better reflect the pattern of economic benefit over the asset life.

findings.paper_title: Essex Pension Fund Advisory Board (PAB) Quarterly Report
findings.headline: Pension fund has received clean Internal Audit opinions for eight consecutive years
findings.detail: Both Funding and Investments and Administration functions received Good Assurance opinions in 2025/26, with no recommendations issued. This extends a run of eight years without any audit findings or recommendations.
findings.matters: A persistent clean audit record across multiple years and functions demonstrates strong financial controls and governance; councils with audit concerns typically attract closer lending scrutiny.
findings.quote: the Fund's Internal Audit outcomes for 2025/26, where both Funding and Investments and Administration received a Good Assurance opinion, with no recommendations issued for the eighth consecutive year.

daily_post.headline: All eight strategic investment risks remain above their target scores
daily_post.lead: Pension fund investment risk reflects on the council's financial governance and asset stewardship; sustained elevation of all strategic risks above target suggests systematic investment challenges that could impair the fund's returns or resilience.
